beats.narration_text: Here's what the skill actually is: a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is called clinical-note-extract-skill. Six items inside — SKILL.md carries the instructions in plain English, and four folders hold assets, references, scripts, and workflows. The file is the program. Claude reads it, then does what it says.

Open the instructions. Four steps, top to bottom. One: define a schema for what to pull. Two: extract candidate values. Three: validate each one — first, check that its span actually appears in the note verbatim, then run further checks per field type. Four: report the result. No branching, unless a step itself says to branch. That linearity is the design choice.

Here's what falls out. Every field it finds comes back with the exact span of text that supports it — provenance built into the output. Every field it can't find comes back as an explicit null, not an inference. Same note, same schema, same output, every run. They optimized for auditability at the expense of coverage: it will never fill in a value the note doesn't literally state, even when a person could reasonably guess.

Clinical-note-extract-skill writes down only what the note literally says, cites the exact text, and marks everything else null. Auditable to a fault, and blind to anything the note doesn't spell out.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: ask it to write a short SKILL.md for a clinical-note-extract skill — schema, extract, validate, report — then feed it a sample note that mentions patient age and chief complaint but not medications. Watch it cite what it can find, and null what it can't. Go deeper: add a 'diagnosis' field, run it twice, and see whether it stays disciplined — or starts inferring a diagnosis from the chief complaint, even when the note never states one.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how a Claude skill does span-level extraction without guessing. A Claude 'skill' is a folder holding SKILL.md — a numbered list of steps Claude reads and runs top to bottom. Write me a short SKILL.md for a CLINICAL-NOTE-EXTRACT skill: four numbered steps (define schema, extract, validate, report) that pulls patient age, chief complaint, and medications from a clinical note. For every field it finds, it must cite the exact substring from the note that supports it. For every field it can't find, it must return null — never an inference. Then draft a two-paragraph sample clinical note that mentions age and chief complaint but not medications. Run the skill on the note and show me the output: each field with its cited span, medications marked null.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: add a 'diagnosis' field to the schema, then feed the same note in twice. Does the skill stay disciplined and return null both times — or does it start inferring a diagnosis from the chief complaint, even when the note never states one?
